title: Affinity Metrics
hook: Look at the same circuit cells by direct wires, then by shared neighbours. Why do the two disagree about which pair is closest?
cardText: Score every pair of cells: direct edge weight, shared neighbours, and pin-count on multi-pin nets. A score ranks pairs; it does not group them.
description: Why direct wires and shared neighbours name different “closest pairs” among the same circuit cells: edge weight, shared neighbours and pin-count.
nextText: Module 03 uses this module’s “summed weight between clusters” to merge.
review: The layer below: a graph’s nodes are cells, and the heavier an edge, the more we want its two ends together; one net can connect three or more cells. [Foundations](../../foundations/index.html)

objectives.text: Explain the difference between scoring (ranking) and grouping (a partition), and why affinity is neither a distance nor a probability.
Compute the direct-weight score by hand and give a stable ranking by (score descending, u, v) that does not depend on input order.
Break a shared-neighbour score into “direct wire + the weaker wire through each shared neighbour”, including pairs with no direct wire.
Explain why a different score changes the first pair to merge (the priority graph: X–Y@5 versus P–Q@8).
Handle wide nets with the clique model’s pin-count: each pair gets w/(|e|−1), so a private two-pin net beats two wide five-pin nets.
Read the pseudocode line by line and implement the three scores in Python.

problem.input: A weighted undirected graph (nodes, edge weights), or a multi-pin netlist (each net is a set of pins with a weight).
problem.output: Every pair with a positive score, as (u, v, score) with u < v, sorted by score descending, then by u and v.
problem.objective: Quantify “how much this pair belongs together” under one **stated** model.
problem.constraints: No self-loops or duplicate edges; a pin repeated inside one net counts once; nets with fewer than two distinct pins are ignored.
problem.assumptions: Edge weights are non-negative and mean connection strength; a shared neighbour x contributes min(w(u,x), w(v,x)); the clique model shares a net out over |e|−1.
problem.stop: Done once every unordered pair has been checked. This module **outputs no groups**; grouping starts in Module 03.

filmNote: The popular-science film starts with group chats, where counting shared chats makes the boss your closest person, then moves to a chip and the three scores. The concise film covers what you must know in about two minutes; the advanced film covers why min, the hub problem, enumeration cost, what pin-count preserves, and the tie rule; the walkthrough, recorded from the real page, takes you through the lab and the code lab. Every score comes from the same engine as this page.
labNote: Switch the score or change one edge’s weight, and the engine recomputes the ranking at once. Stepping through reveals where each pair’s score comes from, in ranking order.
challengeTip: This module’s [Implement] challenge asks you to sort by hand: use the ↑ ↓ on each row to reorder.

mistakes.title: Giving shared-neighbour scores only to pairs that share a wire
mistakes.wrong: The five-node graph lists only 6 pairs, and B–D is missing.
mistakes.why: The shared-neighbour score must check **every** unordered pair; a pair without a direct wire can still have shared neighbours.
mistakes.counter: B–D has no direct wire, but its shared neighbour C gives it min(4, 2) = 2; the full list has 10 pairs.
mistakes.fix: Loop over every u < v, then look up the shared neighbours.

mistakes.title: Thinking every clustering algorithm “merges the top pair first”
mistakes.wrong: Treating this module’s ranking as the common first step of every later module.
mistakes.why: A score is the output of one model. Label propagation changes labels by neighbour votes, spectral bisection sorts by an eigenvector, KL/FM swap or move nodes: none of them merges the top pair.
mistakes.counter: In Module 05’s first round, A takes B’s label; nothing “merges a pair”.
mistakes.fix: Say “greedy merging (Module 03) uses the pair with the highest affinity”, rather than generalising to every algorithm.

mistakes.title: Counting wide nets by occurrences instead of sharing them out
mistakes.wrong: Two five-pin nets (enable, reset) give A–B 2 points, beating E–F on its private net (1 point).
mistakes.why: One five-pin net connects 10 pairs of cells at once, so it says far less about any one pair than a net that connects only E and F.
mistakes.counter: pin-count: A–B = 1/4 + 1/4 = 0.5, E–F = 1/(2−1) = 1, so E–F comes first.
mistakes.fix: State that you use the clique model and divide the weight by |e|−1; do not present it as the only correct model.

mistakes.title: Letting the input decide the order of ties
mistakes.wrong: Feed the edges in reverse and A–B and D–E swap places.
mistakes.why: If you sort by score alone, tied items keep whatever order they had before sorting.
mistakes.counter: A–B and D–E are both 5 (direct weight) or 6 (shared neighbours).
mistakes.fix: Sort by (−score, u, v), and write every pair as u < v.

mistakes.title: Treating affinity as a distance or a probability
mistakes.wrong: Saying “A–B at 6 is three times as close as B–D at 2”, or “A–B are in the same group with 60% probability”.
mistakes.why: Affinity is a ranking score under one model: change the model and the numbers change. It does not satisfy the triangle inequality of a distance, and it is not a probability.
mistakes.counter: The same pair A–B scores 5 by direct weight, 6 by shared neighbours, and something else again on a pin-count netlist.
mistakes.fix: Compare only the order of scores under one model, and say which score you used.

limits:
- The choice of score changes the result of the merging that follows. The three scores here are simple models common in teaching, not the one “best” affinity; real tools may also weigh timing, area or physical distance.
- The shared-neighbour score checks every pair: done naively, n nodes give about n(n−1)/2 pairs. Large netlists need to enumerate along adjacency instead.
- The clique model approximates a multi-pin net: it draws the net as pairwise “illustrative contributions”, and none of those wires exists physically.
- This module outputs no groups; turning a ranking into clusters needs Module 03’s merging rule.

pythonPackage.title: Implement the three scores
pythonPackage.md:
**Task** (three `TODO`s in `starter.py`):

1. `affinity_edge_weight(edges)`: direct weight.
2. `affinity_shared_neighbors(nodes, edges)`: check every unordered pair and list only positive scores.
3. `affinity_pin_count(nodes, nets)`: the clique model; a repeated pin counts once.

All three return `[(u, v, score), ...]` with u < v, sorted by (score descending, u, v).

**Hint 1**: write the double loop over “every unordered pair” first, then decide what each pair adds.

**Hint 2**: a shared neighbour is an x that appears in both u’s and v’s adjacency; it contributes `min(w(u,x), w(v,x))`. The checker also tries a new graph, so memorising the five-node answers will not pass.

kept: Comparing the edge, shared-neighbour and pin-count scores side by side on the same graph.
priority_graph: the first pair to merge changes from X–Y@5 to P–Q@8 (the core example of this module’s challenges and films).
tiny_netlist: two wide five-pin nets and one private net, showing how wide nets dilute.
The exercise ideas of sorting by hand, editing edge weights and “judging only after seeing the breakdown”; the original’s English/French resources remain on the original site as a reference.
